passage:
The corner shop was crowded, and Arnab was counting coins for the fruit when Gopika grabbed a plastic toy drum.
"Buy it, Papa, buy it!"
"Not today."
"Please, please!" Her voice went high and people turned to look.
Arnab crouched down. "Gopika, we have money for the fruit today. The drum costs more than we can spend now."
She wailed and flopped onto the floor. He stayed beside her, waited, and did not buy it.
"We will buy the mangoes, and you can carry the bag."
She hiccupped, took the bag in both arms, and sniffed all the way to the counter.

qa.q: What did Gopika grab in the shop?
qa.a: She grabbed a plastic toy drum.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she flopped onto the floor?
qa.a: She was sad and frustrated because she wanted the drum and did not yet understand price.

qa.q: What went right in how Arnab handled the tantrum?
qa.a: He explained simply that the money was for the fruit, stayed beside her, and did not buy the drum, so crying did not pay.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel with people looking?
qa.a: He may feel a little uneasy, since the shop is crowded and he is short of money, yet he stays calm and keeps to his decision.

grounding: A child begs for a toy, the parent says no and explains money is for the fruit, and does not buy it to stop the tantrum.

passage: At the corner shop near their Pune flat, Harsha spotted a flashing toy car. "Papa, buy it! Please!" Papa, Shankar, looked at the price and shook his head. "Not today." "Why? You have money!" Harsha's voice got louder. People looked. Shankar knelt beside his son. "We have money for the fruit today. The car costs a lot. If I buy it, we can't buy apples and bananas." Harsha scowled. "I don't care about apples." "I know. It's hard to wait." Harsha sulked all the way home, but carried the bag of bananas very carefully.

qa.q: What did Harsha want Papa to buy?
qa.a: Harsha wanted a flashing toy car.

qa.q: Why did Harsha say "You have money!"?
qa.a: He didn't understand price yet and felt frustrated, thinking having money meant Papa could buy anything.

qa.q: How did Shankar explain the no in a way a young child could understand?
qa.a: He said simply that the money was for fruit today and the car cost a lot, and he did not give in when Harsha got louder.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar bought the car to stop the fuss?
qa.a: Harsha would learn that getting loud in shops works, and he'd likely do it again.

grounding: A young boy begs for a toy at a shop, and his father explains simply that the money is for fruit today and doesn't give in.

passage:
"Papa! Papa! That doll! Please!"
"Dilnaz, not today."
"But I want it! Just this one!"
Ujjwal put the tomatoes in the basket. "Today we have money for vegetables and milk. Not for toys."
"But you have lots of money in your phone!"
"The money in the phone is for rent and food and school."
Dilnaz started to cry. "You never buy me anything!"
"I hear you. It's hard." Ujjwal did not buy the doll. He held her hand.
"Can I put it on my birthday list?"
"That's a good idea."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say the money in the phone was for?
qa.a: He said it was for rent and food and school.

qa.q: How was Dilnaz feeling when she said "You never buy me anything!"?
qa.a: She felt upset and frustrated, not yet understanding that money has to be shared between needs.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that a wise parent does?
qa.a: He explained simply what the money was for today, stayed calm and did not buy the doll to stop the crying.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel hearing Dilnaz cry in the shop?
qa.a: He may feel a pang of sadness and pressure, but he stays kind and firm.

grounding: A young girl begs for a doll at a shop, and her father explains simply what the money is for and doesn't give in to the crying.
